newsitem.title: USA: Handful of Fed watchers stick to no-rate-hike guns.
newsitem.headline: Handful of Fed watchers stick to no-rate-hike guns.

text.p: Despite the widespread expectation on Wall Street that the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates next week, a handful of Fed watchers still believe the Fed will not tighten policy, and perhaps leave rates alone throughout 1997.

"If the current inflation environment is benign and (Fed Chairman Alan) Greenspan expects growth to slow to below trend by the end of the year, then there should be no need to tighten," said Ian Shepherdson, chief economist at HSBC Markets Inc, who forecasts a steady Fed policy for 1997.

"It would be masochism for the sake of it," he said, adding that the only reason why the Fed should move is if it truly felt inflation would become a problem and not raising rates would put its credibility at risk. "If they tighten, and they are wrong, they could just reverse it."
Shepherdson is one of eight economists at the 37 primary dealerships who expect the Fed to leave rates steady at Tuesday's policy setting meeting, according to a Reuters poll released Thursday.

Including non-dealers, 34 of 48 Wall Street economists expect a rate hike, well above results of a similar survey a week ago when only 17 of 44 economists predicted a rate hike at the upcoming Fed meeting.

The number of those expecting the Fed to hike rates jumped on Thursday after Greenspan told Congress's Joint Economic Committee that the economy retains a "great deal of vigor," but with no current inflation pressures. Greenspan reiterated that the Fed needs to be "preemptive" in making sure rising wages do not result in inflation at the consumer level.
"He didn't say anything new," Shepherdson said of the testimony. "It's just that a lot of people (economists) decided to be with the rest of the herd."
Mitchell Held, chief economist at Smith Barney Inc, agreed that Greenspan had not changed his tune from his Humphrey-Hawkins testimony last month.
"It's a close call (for a rate hike on Tuesday), but if you look at the testimony, it was balanced," said Held, who also sees the Fed on hold through year-end.
Held said there is very little difference in the economy compared to last July when the "tightening" word first surfaced.
His forecast calls for the economy to slow throughout the rest of the year, as stricter bank lending standards curtail credit availability and high debt levels lead to more subdued consumer spending.
Held also expects the U.S. trade defict to widen, as exports are hampered by a strong dollar and continued weak economies in many of the U.S.'s key trading partners.
Ram Bhagavatula, chief financial economist at Citicorp Securities Markets Inc, citing weak underlying demand, said he saw no reason for the Fed to tighten.

Still, Bhagavatula expects the Fed to tighten on Tuesday, a view he did not hold until Thursday afternoon. "Greenspan said he was going to tighten," he said. "The decision has been in his lap since July.

"But if rates go up they will have to come down that much more," he added, noting he continues to forecast a rate cut sometime in the fourth quarter of this year, with the federal funds rate falling to four to 4.25 percent by the end of 1998. He also predicts 30-year U.S. bond yields diving to 6 percent by the end of 1997.

Bhagavatula argued that the buildup in inventories will lead to lower production later in the year and that retail sales figures were padded early this year by discounting and warmer weather. At the same time, he said inflation will not be a problem.
"A tightening would be a preemptive, preemptive strike," he said. "All it would do is make an already low inflation outlook even lower."
